entries.9b040694a74b52f7e02c25a667dc5768b21d4ed9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv67"/><title type="x-s3">The Excellence of Wisdom.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv67"/> <div sID="gen14397" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Be not thou envious against evil men, neither desire to be with them. <hi type="super">2</hi> For their heart studieth destruction, and their lips talk of mischief. <div eID="gen14397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14398" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. The caution given is much the same with that which we had before (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.17">ch. xxiii. 17</reference>), not to envy sinners, not to think them happy, nor to wish ourselves in their condition, though they prosper ever so much in this world, and are ever so merry and ever so secure. "Let not such a thought ever come into thy mind, O that I could shake off the restraints of religion and conscience, and take as great a liberty to indulge the sensual appetite, as I see such and such do! No; <hi type="italic">desire not to be with them,</hi> to do as they do and fare as they fare, and to <hi type="italic">cast in thy lot among</hi> them." 2. Here is another reason given for this caution: "<hi type="italic">Be not envious against</hi> them, not only because their end will be had, but because their way is so, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.2">v. 2</reference>. Do not think with them, <hi type="italic">for their heart studies destruction</hi> to others, but it will prove destruction to themselves. Do not speak like them, for <hi type="italic">their lips talk of their mischief.</hi> All they say has an ill tendency, to dishonour God, reproach religion, or wrong their neighbour; but it will be mischief to themselves at last. It is therefore thy wisdom to have nothing to do with them. Nor hast thou any reason to look upon them with envy, but with pity rather, or a just indignation at their wicked practices."
entries.dea56583775b7cad397d756ca015edb9d75fd860: <div eID="gen14398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14399" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> Through wisdom is an house builded; and by understanding it is established: <hi type="super">4</hi> And by knowledge shall the chambers be filled with all precious and pleasant riches. 5 A wise man <hi type="italic">is</hi> strong; yea, a man of knowledge increaseth strength. <hi type="super">6</hi> For by wise counsel thou shalt make thy war: and in multitude of counsellors <hi type="italic">there is</hi> safety. <div eID="gen14399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14400" type="x-p"/> We are tempted to envy those that grow rich, and raise their estates and families, by such unjust courses as our consciences will by no means suffer us to use. But, to set aside that temptation, Solomon here shows that a man, with prudent management, may raise his estate and family by lawful and honest means, with a good conscience, and a good name, and the blessing of God upon his industry; and, if the other be raised a little sooner, yet these will last a great deal longer. 1. That which is here recommended to us as having the best influence upon our outward prosperity is <hi type="italic">wisdom,</hi> and <hi type="italic">understanding,</hi> and <hi type="italic">knowledge;</hi> that is, both piety towards God (for that is true wisdom) and prudence in the management of our outward affairs. We must govern ourselves in every thing by the rules of religion first and then of discretion. Some that are truly pious do not thrive in the world, for want of prudence; and some that are prudent enough, yet do not prosper, because they lean to their own understanding and do not acknowledge God in their ways; therefore both must go together to complete a wise man. 2. That which is here set before us as the advantage of true wisdom is that it will make men's outward affairs prosperous and successful. (1.) it will <hi type="italic">build a house and establish it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.24.3">v. 3</reference>. Men may by unrighteous practices build their houses, but they cannot establish them, for the foundation is rotten (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.9-Hab.2.10">Hab. ii. 9, 10</reference>); whereas what is honestly got will wear like steel and be an inheritance to children's children. (2.) It will enrich a house and furnish it, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.4">v. 4</reference>. Those that manage their affairs with wisdom and equity, that are diligent in the use of lawful means for increasing what they have that spare from luxury and spend in charity, are in a fair way to have their shops, their warehouses, their <hi type="italic">chambers, filled with all precious and pleasant riches—precious</hi> because got by honest labour, and <hi type="italic">the substance of a diligent man is precious—pleasant</hi> because enjoyed with holy cheerfulness. Some think this is to be understood chiefly of spiritual riches. <hi type="italic">By knowledge the chambers</hi> of the soul are filled with the graces and comforts of the Spirit, those <hi type="italic">precious and pleasant riches;</hi> for the Spirit, by enlightening the understanding, performs all his other operations on the soul. (3.) It will fortify a house and turn it into a castle: <hi type="italic">Wisdom is better than weapons of war,</hi> offensive or defensive. <hi type="italic">A wise man is in strength,</hi> is in a strong-hold, <hi type="italic">yea, a man of knowledge strengthens might,</hi> that is, increases it, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.5">v. 5</reference>. As we grow in knowledge we grow in all grace, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.18">2 Pet. iii. 18</reference>. Those that <hi type="italic">increase in wisdom</hi> are <hi type="italic">strengthened with all might,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.9">Col. i. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.1.11">11</reference>. A wise man will compass that by his wisdom which a strong man cannot effect by force of arms. The spirit is strengthened both for the spiritual work and the spiritual warfare by true wisdom. (4.) It will govern a house and a kingdom too, and the affairs of both, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.6">v. 6</reference>. Wisdom will erect a college, or council of state. Wisdom will be of use, [1.] For the managing of the public quarrels, so as not to engage in them but for an honest cause and with some probability of success, and, when they are engaged in, to manage them well, and so as to make either an advantageous peace or an honourable retreat: <hi type="italic">By wise counsel thou shalt make war,</hi> which is a thing that may prove of ill consequence if not done by wise counsel. [2.] For the securing of the public peace: <hi type="italic">In the multitude of counsellors there is safety,</hi> for one may foresee the danger, and discern the advantages, which another cannot. In our spiritual conflicts we need wisdom, for our enemy is subtle.  <div eID="gen14400" type="x-p"/>
entries.21da1b6e782167ff1e2047e5d4ec42b39f199e8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv68"/><title type="x-s3">The Malicious and the Scornful.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv68"/> <div sID="gen14401" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Wisdom <hi type="italic">is</hi> too high for a fool: he openeth not his mouth in the gate. <hi type="super">8</hi> He that deviseth to do evil shall be called a mischievous person. <hi type="super">9</hi> The thought of foolishness <hi type="italic">is</hi> sin: and the scorner <hi type="italic">is</hi> an abomination to men. <div eID="gen14401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14402" type="x-p"/> Here is the description, 1. Of a weak man: <hi type="italic">Wisdom is too high</hi> for him; he thinks it so, and therefore, despairing to attain it, he will take no pains in the pursuit of it, but sit down content without it. And really it is so; he has not capacity for it, and therefore the advantages he has for getting it are all in vain to him. It is no easy thing to get wisdom; those that have natural parts good enough, yet if they be foolish, that is, if they be slothful and will not take pains, if they be playful and trifling, and given to their pleasures, if they be viciously inclined and keep bad company, it <hi type="italic">is too high</hi> for them; they are not likely to reach it. And, for want of it, they are unfit for the service of their country: They <hi type="italic">open not their mouth in the gate;</hi> they are not admitted into the council or magistracy, or, if they are, they are dumb statues, and stand for cyphers; they say nothing, because they have nothing to say, and they know that if they should offer any thing it would not be heeded, nay, it would be hissed at. Let young men take pains to get wisdom, that they may be qualified for public business, and do it with reputation. 2. Of a wicked man, who is not only despised as a fool is, but detested. Two sorts of wicked men are so:—(1.) Such as are secretly malicious. Though they speak courteously and conduct themselves plausibly, they <hi type="italic">devise to do evil,</hi> are contriving to do an ill turn to those they bear a grudge to, or have an envious eye at. He that does so <hi type="italic">shall be called a mischievous person,</hi> or <hi type="italic">a master of mischief,</hi> which perhaps was then a common name of reproach; he shall be branded as an <hi type="italic">inventor of evil things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.30">Rom. i. 30</reference>), or if any mischief be done, he shall be suspected as the author of it, or at least accessory to it. This <hi type="italic">devising evil is the thought of foolishness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.24.9">v. 9</reference>. It is made light of, and turned off with a jest, as only a foolish thing, but really it <hi type="italic">is sin,</hi> it is exceedingly sinful; you cannot call it by a worse name than to call it <hi type="italic">sin.</hi> It is bad to do evil, but it is worse to devise it; for that has in it the subtlety and poison of the old serpent. But it may be taken more generally. We contract guilt, not only by the act of foolishness, but by the thought of it, though it go no further; the first risings of sin in the heart are sin, offensive to God, and must be repented of or we are undone. Not only malicious, unclean, proud thoughts, but even foolish thoughts, are sinful thoughts. If <hi type="italic">vain thoughts lodge in the heart,</hi> they defile it (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.14">Jer. iv. 14</reference>), which is a reason why we should <hi type="italic">keep our hearts with all diligence,</hi> and harbour no thoughts there which cannot give a good account of themselves, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.5">Gen. vi. 5</reference>. (2.) Such as are openly abusive: <hi type="italic">The scorner,</hi> who gives ill-language to every body, takes a pleasure in affronting people and reflecting upon them, <hi type="italic">is an abomination to men;</hi> none that have any sense of honour and virtue will care to keep company with him. <hi type="italic">The seat of the scornful</hi> is the <hi type="italic">pestilential chair</hi> (as the LXX. calls it, <reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Ps. i. 1</reference>), which no wise man will come near, for fear of taking the infection. Those that strive to make others odious do but make themselves so.
entries.caedcfc7bae2fea8b552219cd609709f87721f3b: <div eID="gen14402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14403" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> <hi type="italic">If</hi> thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength <hi type="italic">is</hi> small. <div eID="gen14403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14404" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. In <hi type="italic">the day of adversity</hi> we are apt to <hi type="italic">faint,</hi> to droop and be discouraged, to desist from our work, and to despair of relief. Our spirits sink, and then our hands hang down and our knees grow feeble, and we become unfit for anything. And often those that are most cheerful when they are well droop most, and are most dejected, when any thing ails them. 2. This is an evidence that our <hi type="italic">strength is small,</hi> and is a means of weakening it more. "It is a sign that thou art not a man of any resolution, any firmness of thought, any consideration, any faith (for that is the strength of a soul), if thou canst not bear up under an afflictive change of thy condition." Some are so feeble that they can bear nothing; if a trouble does but <hi type="italic">touch</hi> them (<reference osisRef="Job.4.5">Job iv. 5</reference>), nay, if it does but threaten them, they faint immediately and are ready to give up all for gone; and by this means they render themselves unfit to grapple with their trouble and unable to help themselves. <hi type="italic">Be of good courage</hi> therefore, <hi type="italic">and God shall strengthen thy heart.</hi>  <div eID="gen14404" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb66a32b492060126cd21115d63492b0ebd2f7a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv69"/><title type="x-s3">Pleasure and Advantages of Wisdom.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv69"/> <div sID="gen14405" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> If thou forbear to deliver <hi type="italic">them that are</hi> drawn unto death, and <hi type="italic">those that are</hi> ready to be slain; <hi type="super">12</hi> If thou sayest, Behold, we knew it not; doth not he that pondereth the heart consider <hi type="italic">it?</hi> and he that keepeth thy soul, doth <hi type="italic">not</hi> he know <hi type="italic">it?</hi> and shall <hi type="italic">not</hi> he render to <hi type="italic">every</hi> man according to his works? <div eID="gen14405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14406" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A great duty required of us, and that is to appear for the relief of oppressed innocency. If we see the lives or livelihoods of any in danger of being taken away unjustly, we ought to bestir ourselves all we can to save them, by disproving the false accusations on which they are condemned and seeking out proofs of their innocency. Though the persons be not such as we are under any particular obligation to, we must help them, out of a general zeal for justice. If any be set upon by force and violence, and it be in our power to rescue them, we ought to do it. Nay, if we see any through ignorance exposing themselves to danger, or fallen in distress, as travellers upon the road, ships at sea, or any the like, it is our duty, though it be with peril to ourselves, to hasten with help to them and not <hi type="italic">forbear to deliver them,</hi> not to be slack, or remiss, or indifferent, in such a case. 2. An answer to the excuse that is commonly make for the omission of this duty. Thou wilt say, "<hi type="italic">Behold, we knew it not;</hi> we were not aware of the imminency of the danger the person was in; we could not be sure that he was innocent, nor did we know how to prove his innocence, nor which way to do any thing in favour of him, else we would have helped him." Now, (1.) It is easy to make such an excuse as this, sufficient to avoid the censures of men, for perhaps they cannot disprove us when we say, <hi type="italic">We knew it not,</hi> or, <hi type="italic">We forgot;</hi> and the temptation to tell a lie for the excusing of a fault is very strong when we know that it is impossible to be disproved, the truth lying wholly in our own breast, as when we say, <hi type="italic">We thought so and so, and really designed it,</hi> which no one is conscious of but ourselves. (2.) It is not so easy with such excuses to evade the judgment of God; and to the discovery of that we lie open and by the determination of that we must abide. Now, [1.] God <hi type="italic">ponders the heart and keeps the soul;</hi> he keeps an eye upon it, observes all the motions of it; its most secret thoughts and intents are all naked and open before him. It is his prerogative to do so, and that in which he glories. <reference osisRef="Jer.17.10">Jer. xvii. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">I the Lord search the heart.</hi> He <hi type="italic">keeps the soul,</hi> holds it in life. This is a good reason why we should be tender of the lives of others, and do all we can to preserve them, because our lives have been precious in the sight of God and he has graciously kept them. [2.] He knows and considers whether the excuse we make be true or no, whether it was because we did not know it or whether the true reason was not because we did not love our neighbour as we ought, but were selfish, and regardless both of God and man. Let this serve to silence all our frivolous pleas, by which we think to stop the mouth of conscience when it charges us with the omission of plain duty: <hi type="italic">Does not he that ponders the heart consider it?</hi> [3.] He will judge us accordingly. As his knowledge cannot be imposed upon, so his justice cannot be biassed, but he will <hi type="italic">render to every man according to his works,</hi> not only the commission of evil works, but the omission of good works.
entries.ad6e45bd191ea5130ac82cc556244c9bf6f36ce4: <div eID="gen14406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14407" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> My son, eat thou honey, because <hi type="italic">it is</hi> good; and the honeycomb, <hi type="italic">which is</hi> sweet to thy taste: <hi type="super">14</hi> So <hi type="italic">shall</hi> the knowledge of wisdom <hi type="italic">be</hi> unto thy soul: when thou hast found <hi type="italic">it,</hi> then there shall be a reward, and thy expectation shall not be cut off. <div eID="gen14407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14408" type="x-p"/> We are here quickened to the study of wisdom by the consideration both of the pleasure and the profit of it. 1. It will be very pleasant. We <hi type="italic">eat honey because it is sweet to the taste,</hi> and upon that account we call it <hi type="italic">good,</hi> especially that which runs first from the <hi type="italic">honey-comb.</hi> Canaan was said to flow with milk and honey, and honey was the common food of the country (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.41-Luke.24.42">Luke xxiv. 41, 42</reference>), even for children, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.15">Isa. vii. 15</reference>. Thus should we feed upon wisdom, and relish the good instructions of it. Those that have tasted honey need no further proof that it is sweet, nor can they by any argument be convinced of the contrary; so those that have experienced the power of truth and godliness are abundantly satisfied of the pleasure of both; they have tasted the sweetness of them, and all the atheists in the world with their sophistry, and the profane with their banter, cannot alter their sentiments. 2. It will be very profitable. Honey may be <hi type="italic">sweet to the taste</hi> and yet not wholesome, but wisdom has a future recompence attending it, as well as a present sweetness in it. "Thou art permitted to <hi type="italic">eat honey,</hi> and the agreeableness of it to thy taste invites thee to it; but thou hast much more reason to relish and digest the precepts <hi type="italic">of wisdom,</hi> for <hi type="italic">when thou hast found</hi> that, <hi type="italic">there shall be a reward;</hi> thou shalt be paid for thy pleasure, while the servants of sin pay dearly for their pains. Wisdom does indeed set thee to work, but <hi type="italic">there shall be a reward;</hi> it does indeed raise great expectations in thee, but as thy labour, so thy hope, shall not be in vain; <hi type="italic">thy expectation shall not be cut off</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.18">ch. xxiii. 18</reference>), nay, it shall be infinitely outdone."  <div eID="gen14408" type="x-p"/>
entries.9945f1e97957f93a5b5f49f1a4c311a659f8a509: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv70"/><title type="x-s3">Cautions against Envy.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv70"/> <div sID="gen14409" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Lay not wait, O wicked <hi type="italic">man,</hi> against the dwelling of the righteous; spoil not his resting place: <hi type="super">16</hi> For a just <hi type="italic">man</hi> falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief. <div eID="gen14409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14410" type="x-p"/> This is spoken, not so much by way of counsel to wicked men (they will not receive instruction, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.9">ch. xxiii. 9</reference>), but rather in defiance of them, for the encouragement of good people that are threatened by them. See here, 1. The designs of the wicked against the righteous, and the success they promise themselves in those designs. The plot is laid deeply: They <hi type="italic">lay wait against the dwelling of the righteous,</hi> thinking to charge some iniquity upon it, or compass some design against it; they lie in wait at the door, to catch him when he stirs out, as David's persecutors, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.1">Ps. lix.</reference> <hi type="italic">title.</hi> The hope is raised high; they doubt not but to <hi type="italic">spoil his dwelling-place</hi> because he is weak and cannot support it, because his condition is low and distressed, and he is almost down already. All this is a fruit of the old enmity in the seed of the serpent against the seed of the woman. <hi type="italic">The blood-thirsty hate the upright.</hi> 2. The folly and frustration of these designs (1.) The righteous man, whose ruin was expected, recovers himself. He <hi type="italic">falls seven times</hi> into trouble, but, by the blessing of God upon his wisdom and integrity, he <hi type="italic">rises again,</hi> sees through his troubles and sees better times after them. The <hi type="italic">just man falls,</hi> sometimes <hi type="italic">falls seven times</hi> perhaps, into sin, sins of infirmity, through the surprise of temptation; but he <hi type="italic">rises again</hi> by repentance, finds mercy with God, and regains his peace. (2.) <hi type="italic">The wicked</hi> man, who expected to see his ruin and to help it forward, is undone. He <hi type="italic">falls into mischief;</hi> his sins and his troubles are his utter destruction.
entries.be84637558469d99dd61f926e76d45011313b81c: <div eID="gen14410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14411" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth: <hi type="super">18</hi> Lest the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> see <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and it displease him, and he turn away his wrath from him. <div eID="gen14411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14412" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. The pleasure we are apt to take in the troubles of an enemy is forbidden us. If any have done us an ill turn, or if we bear them ill-will only because they stand in our light or in our way, when any damage comes to them (suppose they fall), or any danger (suppose they stumble), our corrupt hearts are too apt to conceive a secret delight and satisfaction in it—<hi type="italic">Aha! so would we have it; they are entangled; the wilderness has shut them in</hi>—or, as Tyrus said concerning Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.2">Ezek. xxvi. 2</reference>) <hi type="italic">I shall be replenished, now she is laid waste.</hi> "Men hope in the ruin of their enemies or rivals to wreak their revenge or to find their account; but be not thou so inhuman; <hi type="italic">rejoice not when</hi> the worst <hi type="italic">enemy</hi> thou hast <hi type="italic">falls.</hi>" There may be a holy joy in the destruction of God's enemies, as it tends to the glory of God and the welfare of the church (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.10">Ps. lviii. 10</reference>); but in the ruin of our enemies, as such, we must by no means rejoice; on the contrary, we must weep even with them when they weep (as David, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.13-Ps.35.14">Ps. xxxv. 13, 14</reference>), and that in sincerity, not so much as letting our hearts be secretly glad at their calamities. 2. The provocation which that pleasure gives to God is assigned as the reason of that prohibition: <hi type="italic">The Lord</hi> will <hi type="italic">see it,</hi> though it be hidden in the heart only, <hi type="italic">and it</hi> will <hi type="italic">displease him,</hi> as it will displease a prudent father to see one child triumph in the correction of another, which he ought to tremble at, and take warning by, not knowing how soon it may be his own case, he having so often deserved it. Solomon adds an argument <hi type="italic">ad hominem—addressed to the individual:</hi> "Thou canst not do a greater kindness to <hi type="italic">thy enemy,</hi> when he has fallen, than to rejoice in it; for them, to cross thee and vex thee, God will <hi type="italic">turn his wrath from him;</hi> for, as <hi type="italic">the wrath of man works not the righteousness of God,</hi> so the righteousness of God was never intended to gratify the wrath of man, and humour his foolish passions; rather than seem to do that he will adjourn the execution of his wrath: nay, it is implied that when he <hi type="italic">turns his wrath from him</hi> he will turn it against thee and the cup of trembling shall be put into thy hand."
entries.d58dc6dbde5f80dbeb2754c58b8a5a663dfbcb08: <div eID="gen14412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14413" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> Fret not thyself because of evil <hi type="italic">men,</hi> neither be thou envious at the wicked; <hi type="super">20</hi> For there shall be no reward to the evil <hi type="italic">man;</hi> the candle of the wicked shall be put out. <div eID="gen14413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14414" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. He repeats the caution he had before given against envying the pleasures and successes of wicked man in their wicked ways. This he quotes from his father David, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.1">Ps. xxxvii. 1</reference>. We must not in any case <hi type="italic">fret</hi> ourselves, or make ourselves uneasy, whatever God does in his providence how disagreeable soever it is to our sentiments, interests, and expectations, we must acquiesce in it. Even that which grieves us must not <hi type="italic">fret</hi> us; nor must our eye be evil against any because God is good. Are we more wise or just than he? If wicked people prosper, we must not therefore incline to do as they do. 2. He gives a reason for this caution, taken from the end of that way which wicked man walk in. Envy not their prosperity; for, (1.) There is no true happiness in it: <hi type="italic">Thee shall be no reward to the evil man;</hi> his prosperity only serves for his present subsistence; these are all the good things he must ever expect: there is none intended him in the world of retribution. <hi type="italic">He has his reward,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.2">Matt. vi. 2</reference>. He shall have none. Those are not to be envied that have their portion in this life and must out-live it, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 14</reference>. (2.) There is no continuance in it; their <hi type="italic">candle</hi> shines brightly, but it shall presently <hi type="italic">be put out,</hi> and a final period put to all their comforts, <reference osisRef="Job.21.14">Job xxi. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.1-Ps.37.2">Ps. xxxvii. 1, 2</reference>.  <div eID="gen14414" type="x-p"/>
entries.6cbcd2550a8584d91f02d0fe6f1a0927cb098d30: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv71"/><title type="x-s3">Counsel to Magistrates.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv71"/> <div sID="gen14415" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> My son, fear thou the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> and the king: <hi type="italic">and</hi> meddle not with them that are given to change: <hi type="super">22</hi> For their calamity shall rise suddenly; and who knoweth the ruin of them both? <div eID="gen14415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14416" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Religion and loyalty must go together. As men, it is our duty to honour our Creator, to worship and reverence him, and to be always in his fear; as members of a community, incorporated for mutual benefit, it is our duty to be faithful and dutiful to the government God has set over us, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.1-Rom.13.2">Rom. xiii. 1, 2</reference>. Those that are truly religious will be loyal, in conscience towards God; the godly in the land will be the <hi type="italic">quiet in the land;</hi> and those are not truly loyal, or will be so no longer than is for their interest, that are not religious. How should he be true to his prince that is false to his God? And, if they come in competition, it is an adjudged case, we must <hi type="italic">obey God rather than men.</hi> 2. Innovations in both are to be dreaded. Have nothing to do, he does not say, with those that <hi type="italic">change,</hi> for there may be cause to change for the better, but <hi type="italic">those that are given to change,</hi> that affect change for change-sake, out of a peevish discontent with that which is and a fondness for novelty, or a desire to fish in troubled waters: <hi type="italic">Meddle not with those that are given to change</hi> either in religion or in a civil government; <hi type="italic">come not into their secret;</hi> join not with them in their cabals, nor enter into the mystery of their iniquity. 3. Those that are of restless, factious, turbulent spirits, commonly pull mischief upon their own heads ere they are aware: <hi type="italic">Their calamity shall rise suddenly.</hi> Though they carry on their designs with the utmost secresy, they will be discovered, and brought to condign punishment, when they little think of it. <hi type="italic">Who knows</hi> the time and manner of <hi type="italic">the ruin</hi> which both God and the king will bring on their contemners, <hi type="italic">both</hi> on them and those that meddle with them?
entries.0988bc5127a1a66743e0b5c3aa03a119e83067d7: <div eID="gen14416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14417" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> These <hi type="italic">things</hi> also <hi type="italic">belong</hi> to the wise. <hi type="italic">It is</hi> not good to have respect of persons in judgment. 24 He that saith unto the wicked, Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> righteous; him shall the people curse, nations shall abhor him: <hi type="super">25</hi> But to them that rebuke <hi type="italic">him</hi> shall be delight, and a good blessing shall come upon them. <hi type="super">26</hi> <hi type="italic">Every man</hi> shall kiss <hi type="italic">his</hi> lips that giveth a right answer. <div eID="gen14417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14418" type="x-p"/> Here are lessons for <hi type="italic">wise</hi> men, that is, judges and princes. As subjects must do their duty, and be obedient to magistrates, so magistrates must do their duty in administering justice to their subjects, both in pleas of the crown and causes between party and party. These are lessons for them. 1. They must always weigh the merits of a cause, and not be swayed by any regard, one way or other, to the parties concerned: <hi type="italic">It is not good</hi> in itself, nor can it ever do well, <hi type="italic">to have respect of persons in judgment;</hi> the consequences of it cannot but be the perverting of justice and doing wrong under colour of law and equity. A good judge will know the truth, not know faces, so as to countenance a friend and help him out in a bad cause, or so much as omit any thing that can be said or done in favour of a righteous cause, when it is the cause of an enemy. 2. They must never connive at or encourage wicked people in their wicked practices. Magistrates in their places, and ministers in theirs, are to deal faithfully and the wicked man, though he be a great man or a particular friend, to convict him of his wickedness, to show him what will be in the end thereof, to discover him to others, that they may avoid him. But if those whose office it is thus to show people their transgressions palliate them and connive at them, if they excuse the wicked man, much more if they prefer him and associate with him (which is, in effect, to say, <hi type="italic">Thou art righteous</hi>), they shall justly be looked upon as enemies to the public peace and welfare, which they ought to advance, and <hi type="italic">the people shall curse them</hi> and cry out shame on them; and even those of other <hi type="italic">nations shall abhor them,</hi> as base betrayers of their trust. 3. They must discountenance and give check to all fraud, violence, injustice, and immorality; and, though thereby they may disoblige a particular person, yet they will recommend themselves to the favour of God and man. Let magistrates and ministers, and private persons too that are capable of doing it, <hi type="italic">rebuke</hi> the wicked, that they may bring them to repentance or put them to shame, and they shall have the comfort of it in their own bosoms: <hi type="italic">To them shall be delight,</hi> when their consciences witness for them that they have been witnesses for God; <hi type="italic">and a good blessing shall come upon them,</hi> the blessing of God and good men; they shall be deemed religion's patrons and their country's patriots. See <reference osisRef="Prov.28.23">ch. xxviii. 23</reference>. 4. They must always give judgment according to equity (<reference osisRef="Prov.24.26">v. 26</reference>); they must <hi type="italic">give a right answer,</hi> that is, give their opinion and pass sentence according to law and them true merits of the cause; and <hi type="italic">every one shall kiss his lips that</hi> does so, that is, shall love and honour him, and be subject to his orders, for there is a kiss of allegiance as well as of affection. He that in common conversation likewise speaks pertinently and with sincerity recommends himself to his company and is beloved and respected by all.
entries.7daa564fe39acac825ee358f94a878566e802da1: <div eID="gen14418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14419" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> Prepare thy work without, and make it fit for thyself in the field; and afterwards build thine house. <div eID="gen14419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14420" type="x-p"/> This is a rule of prudence in the management of household affairs; for all good men should be good husbands, and manage with discretion, which would prevent a great deal of sin, and trouble, and disgrace to their profession. 1. We must prefer necessaries before conveniences, and not lay that out for show which should be expended for the support of the family. We must be contented with a mean cottage for a habitation, rather than want, or go in debt for, food convenient. 2. We must not think of building till we can afford it: "First apply thyself to <hi type="italic">thy work without in the field;</hi> let thy ground be put into good order; look after thy husbandry, for it is that by which thou must get; and, when thou hast got well by that, then, and not till then, thou mayest think of rebuilding and beautifying <hi type="italic">thy house,</hi> for that is it upon which, and in which, thou wilt have occasion to spend." Many have ruined their estates and families by laying out money on that which brings nothing in, beginning <hi type="italic">to build</hi> when they were <hi type="italic">not able to finish.</hi> Some understand it as advice to young men not to marry (for by that the house is built) till they have set up in the world, and not wherewith to maintain a wife and children comfortably. 3. When we have any great design on foot it is wisdom to take it before us, and make the necessary preparations, before we fall to work, that, when it is begun, it may not stand still for want of materials. Solomon observed this rule himself in building the house of God; all was made ready <hi type="italic">before it was brought to the ground,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.7">1 Kings vi. 7</reference>.
entries.c74261ef92a49c9fb3e8b9ea4149ecbef007d21f: <div eID="gen14420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14421" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> Be not a witness against thy neighbour without cause; and deceive <hi type="italic">not</hi> with thy lips. <hi type="super">29</hi> Say not, I will do so to him as he hath done to me: I will render to the man according to his work. <div eID="gen14421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14422" type="x-p"/> We are here forbidden to be in any thing injurious to our neighbour, particularly in and by the forms of law, either, 1. As <hi type="italic">a witness:</hi> "Never bear a testimony against any man <hi type="italic">without cause,</hi> unless what thou sayest thou knowest to be punctually true and thou hast a clear call to testify it. Never bear a false testimony against any one;" for it follows, "<hi type="italic">Deceive not with thy lips;</hi> deceive not the judge and jury, deceive not those whom thou conversest with, into an ill opinion of thy neighbour. When thou speakest of thy neighbour do not only speak that which is true, but take heed lest, in the manner of thy speaking, thou insinuate any thing that is otherwise and so shouldst deceive by innuendos or hyperboles." Or, 2. As a plaintiff or prosecutor. If there be occasion to bring an action or information against thy neighbour, let it not be from a spirit of revenge. "<hi type="italic">Say not,</hi> I am resolved I will be even with him: <hi type="italic">I will do so to him as he had done to me.</hi>" Even a righteous cause becomes unrighteous when it is thus prosecuted with malice. <hi type="italic">Say not, I will render to the man according to his work,</hi> and make him pay dearly for it; for it is God's prerogative to do so, and we must leave it to him, and not step into his throne, or take his work out of his hands. If we will needs be our own carvers, and judges in our own cause, we forfeit the benefit of an appeal to God's tribunal; therefore we must not avenge ourselves, because he has said, <hi type="italic">Vengeance is mine.</hi>  <div eID="gen14422" type="x-p"/>
entries.3624c4fa9c7e6efcd381f96548d505023614783a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv72"/><title type="x-s3">The Vineyard of the Slothful.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv72"/> <div sID="gen14423" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> I went by the field of the slothful, and by the vineyard of the man void of understanding; <hi type="super">31</hi> And, lo, it was all grown over with thorns, <hi type="italic">and</hi> nettles had covered the face thereof, and the stone wall thereof was broken down. 32 Then I saw, <hi type="italic">and</hi> considered <hi type="italic">it</hi> well: I looked upon <hi type="italic">it, and</hi> received instruction. 33 <hi type="italic">Yet</hi> a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: <hi type="super">34</hi> So shall thy poverty come <hi type="italic">as</hi> one that travelleth; and thy want as an armed man. <div eID="gen14423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14424" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The view which Solomon took of <hi type="italic">the field and vineyard of the slothful</hi> man. He did not go on purpose to see it, but, as he passed by, observing the fruitfulness of the ground, as it is very proper for travellers to do, and his subjects' management of their land, as it is very proper for magistrates to do, he cast his eye upon a <hi type="italic">field</hi> and a <hi type="italic">vineyard</hi> unlike all the rest; for, though the soil was good, yet there was nothing growing in them but <hi type="italic">thorns and nettles,</hi> not here and there one, but they were all overrun with weeds; and, if there had been any fruit, it would have been eaten up by the beasts, for there was no fence: <hi type="italic">The stone-wall was broken down</hi> See the effects of that curse upon the ground (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.18">Gen. iii. 18</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Thorns and thistles shall it bring forth unto thee,</hi> and nothing else unless thou take pains with it." See what a blessing to the world the husbandman's calling is, and what a wilderness this earth, even Canaan itself, would be without it. <hi type="italic">The king himself is served of the field,</hi> but he would be ill served if God did not teach the husbandman discretion and diligence to clear the ground, plant it, sow it, and fence it. See what a great difference there is between some and others in the management even of their worldly affairs, and how little some consult their reputation, not caring though they proclaim their slothfulness, in the manifest effects of it, to all that pass by, shamed by their neighbour's diligence. 2. The reflections which he made upon it. He paused a little <hi type="italic">and considered it, looked</hi> again <hi type="italic">upon it, and received instruction.</hi> He did not break out into any passionate censures of the owner, did not call him any ill names, but he endeavoured himself to get good by the observation and to be quickened by it to diligence. Note, Those that are to give instruction to others must receive instruction themselves, and instruction may be received, not only from what we read and hear, but from what we see, not only from what we see of the works of God, but from what we see of the manners of man, not only from men's good manners, but from their evil manners. Plutarch relates a saying of Cato Major, "That wise men profit more by fools than fools by wise men; for wise men will avoid the faults of fools, but fools will not imitate the virtues of wise men." Solomon reckoned that he <hi type="italic">received instruction</hi> by this sight, though it did not suggest to him any new notion or lesson, but only put him in mind of an observation he himself had formerly made, both of the ridiculous folly of the sluggard (who, when he has needful work to do, lies dozing in bed and cries, <hi type="italic">Yet a little sleep, a little slumber,</hi> and still it will be a little more, till he has slept his eyes out, and, instead of being fitted by sleep for business, as wise men are, he is dulled, and stupefied, and made good for nothing) and of certain misery that attends him: his <hi type="italic">poverty comes as one that travels;</hi> it is constantly coming nearer and nearer to him, and will be upon him speedily, and want seizes him as irresistibly <hi type="italic">as an armed man,</hi> a highwayman that will strip him of all he has. Now this is applicable, not only to our worldly business, to show what a scandalous thing slothfulness in that is, and how injurious to the family, but to the affairs of our souls. Note, (1.) Our souls are our fields and vineyards, which we are every one of us to take care of, to dress, and to keep. They are capable of being improved with good husbandry; that may be got out of them which will be fruit abounding to our account. We are charged with them, to occupy them till our Lord come; and a great deal of care and pains it is requisite that we should take about them. (2.) These fields and vineyards are often in a very bad state, not only no fruit brought forth, but all overgrown with <hi type="italic">thorns</hi> and <hi type="italic">nettles</hi> (scratching, stinging, inordinate lusts and passions, pride, covetousness, sensuality, malice, those are the thorns and nettles, the wild grapes, which the unsanctified heart produces), no guard kept against the enemy, but the <hi type="italic">stone-wall broken down,</hi> and all lies in common, all exposed. (3.) Where it is thus it is owing to the sinner's own slothfulness and folly. He is a sluggard, loves sleep, hates labour; and he is void of understanding, understands neither his business nor his interest; he is perfectly besotted. (4.) The issue of it will certainly be the ruin of the soul and all its welfare. It is everlasting want that thus comes upon it as an armed man. We know the place assigned to the wicked and slothful servant.  <chapter eID="Prov.24"/> <div eID="gen14424" type="x-p"/>

Especially avoid retaliation (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.43-Matt.5.45">Mt 5:43-45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.17">Ro 12:17</reference>). <div eID="gen12071" type="x-p"/>
entries.c160fccd724fc0700f1c9e50f6beff23b1928c87: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7803"/><div sID="gen12072" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7803"/>30-31. A striking picture of the effects of sloth. <div eID="gen12072" type="x-p"/>
entries.8dc3df3045398581d2b7e5458bf90a8c2433cca5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7804"/><div sID="gen12073" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7804"/>32-34. From the folly of the sluggard learn wisdom (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.10">Pr 6:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.11">11</reference>). <chapter eID="Prov.24"/>

entries.e8436d4f4107684c84f8d00cb2a1246f4d91f19f: <div eID="gen24704" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen24705" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24706" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24706" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24705" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24707" type="x-p"/> Do not be envious. Of the house wisely built. Counsel necessary in war. Save life when thou canst. Of honey and the honey-comb. Of the just that falleth seven times. We should not rejoice at the misfortune of others. Ruin of the wicked. Fear God and the king. Prepare thy work. The field of the sluggard, and the vineyard of the foolish, described.
entries.f5b4f77cddadc2e231fcfc4adad3605fc0a59fd7: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen24707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24708" type="x-p"/> Through wisdom is a house blinded - That is, a family; household affairs. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Pro.9.1">Pro 9:1</reference> (note), etc.
entries.76901f41a4b33b86a4d05ad36ffd7f743154575f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen24708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24709" type="x-p"/> A wise man is strong - His wisdom enables him to construct a great variety of machines, by which, under his own influence, he can do the labor of a hundred or even a thousand men. But in all cases wisdom gives power and influence; and he who is wise to salvation can overcome even Satan himself. The Septuagint has: "The wise is better than the strong; and the man who has prudence, than a stout husbandman."
entries.162625a7f88cdf2eb0509c1d4ffb78fdfc4cdf34: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen24709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24710" type="x-p"/> By wise counsel thou shalt make thy war - See note on <reference osisRef="Pro.20.18">Pro 20:18</reference>.
entries.181c6c21fc0fd6db2b13abb58bd552eb52b5ad99: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen24710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24711" type="x-p"/> A fool - openeth not his mouth in the gate - Is not put into public offices of trust and responsibility.
entries.866adca70cd0a45dcbf7eefbb57fbdc3719f6ff7: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen24711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24712" type="x-p"/> The thought of foolishness is sin - זמת אולת חטאת zimmath ivveleth chattath. "The device of folly is transgression;" or, "an evil purpose is sinful;" or, perhaps more literally, "the device of the foolish is sin." It has been variously understood by the versions. "The cunning: of the fool is sin." - Targum. "The imprudent man (or fool, αφρων) shall die in sins." - Septuagint. <div eID="gen24712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24713" type="x-p"/> So the Arabic. <div eID="gen24713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24714" type="x-p"/> The thinkynge of the fool is synne - Old MS. Bible. <div eID="gen24714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24715" type="x-p"/> Fool is here taken for a wicked man, who is not only evil in his actions, but every thought of his heart is evil, and that continually. A simple thought about foolishness, or about sin itself, is not sinful; it is the purpose or device, the harbouring evil thoughts, and devising how to sin, that is criminal.
entries.aaa89d7777c518faa0ed8765d2557e840679f8fa: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen24715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24716" type="x-p"/> If thou faint - If thou give way to discouragement and despair in the day of adversity - time of trial or temptation. <div eID="gen24716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24717" type="x-p"/> Thy strength is small - צר כחכה tsar cochachah, thy strength is contracted. So the old MS. Bible excellently: Gif sliden thou dispeire, in the dai of anguyfs, schal be made litil thy strengthe. In times of trial we should endeavor to be doubly courageous; when a man loses his courage, his strength avails him nothing.
entries.a25b1f7ffbe3b911e5174523274b8df2b80c3540: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen24717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24718" type="x-p"/> If thou forbear to deliver - If thou seest the innocent taken by the hand of lawless power or superstitious zeal, and they are about to be put to death, thou shouldst rise up in their behalf, boldly plead for them, testify to their innocence when thou knowest it; and thus thou wilt not be guilty of blood; which thou wouldst be, if, through any pretense, thou shouldst neglect to save the life of a man unjustly condemned.
entries.8220a38534073d6f774012a0923b2f518e43243b: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen24718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24719" type="x-p"/> And the honey-comb - I have often had occasion to remark how much finer the flavour of honey is in the honey-comb than it is after it has been expressed from it, and exposed to the action of the air. But it has been asserted that the honey-comb is never eaten; it must be by those who have no acquaintance with the apiary. I have seen the comb with its contained honey eaten frequently, and of it I have repeatedly partaken. And that our Lord ate it, is evident from <reference osisRef="Luk.24.42">Luk 24:42</reference>. Nor can any man who has not eaten it in this way feel the full force of the allusions to the honey-comb and its sweetness in several parts of the sacred writings. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.27">1Sam 14:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.19.10">Psa 19:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Pro.5.3">Pro 5:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Pro.16.24">Pro 16:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Pro.27.7">Pro 27:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Sol.4.11">Sol 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Sol.5.1">Sol 5:1</reference>; and the place before us.
entries.f893a062560d23c354bee4be8dd88c870ddc17ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen24719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24720" type="x-p"/> So shall the knowledge of wisdom be unto thy soul - True religion, experimental godliness, shall be to thy soul as the honey-comb is to thy mouth. <div eID="gen24720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24721" type="x-p"/> Then there shall be a reward, and thy expectation shall not be cut off - This is precisely the same with that in <reference osisRef="Pro.23.18">Pro 23:18</reference> (note), where see the note. The word אחרית acharith, we translate in the former place an end, and here we translate it a reward; but there is no place I believe in the sacred writings in which it has any such acceptation; nor can such a meaning be deduced from the root אחר achar, which always refers to behind, after, extremity, latter part, time, etc., but never carries the idea of recompense, compensation, or such like; nor has one of the versions understood it so. There is another state or life, and thy expectation of happiness in a future world shall not be cut off. In this sense the versions all understood it. I will take them as they lie before me. "Which (wisdom) when thou shalt have found, thou shalt have hope in thy last days; and thy hope shall not perish." - Vulgate. "And if thou find it, thou shalt have a good death; and hope shall not forsake thee." - Septuagint. "Which, if thou have found, thy latter days shall be better than the former; and thy hope shall not be consumed." - Chaldee. "There shall be an end, and thy hope shall not be cut off." - Syriac. "For, if thou shalt find her, (wisdom), thy death shall be glorious, and thy hope will not fail thee." - Arabic. <div eID="gen24721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24722" type="x-p"/> Whiche whan thou fyndist schalt han in the last thingis, hope: and thin hope schal not perischen - Old MS. Bible. "And there is Good Hope; yee that hope shal not be in vayne." - Coverdale. <div eID="gen24722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24723" type="x-p"/> This rendering is indefinite, which is not the usual custom of the translator.
entries.0a6a4cf746344cad07763c51a54a429026422aaf: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen24723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24724" type="x-p"/> The dwelling of the righteous - צדיק tsaddik, the man who is walking unblameably in all the testimonies of God; who is rendering to every man his due.
entries.a7bd3580e6d7bf17d0a3e846fdf4c2737ccc23c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen24724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24725" type="x-p"/> For a just man - צדיק tsaddik, the righteous, the same person mentioned above. <div eID="gen24725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24726" type="x-p"/> Falleth seven times - Gets very often into distresses through his resting place being spoiled by the wicked man, the robber, the spoiler of the desert, lying in wait for this purpose, <reference osisRef="Pro.24.15">Pro 24:15</reference>. <div eID="gen24726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24727" type="x-p"/> And riseth up again - Though God permit the hand of violence sometimes to spoil his tent, temptations to assail his mind, and afflictions to press down his body, he constantly emerges; and every time he passes through the furnace, he comes out brighter and more refined. <div eID="gen24727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24728" type="x-p"/> But the wicked shall fall into mischief - And there they shall lie; having no strong arm to uphold them. Yet,
entries.b7c365580e0404158dffc1160bf4f78664f95db2: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen24728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24729" type="x-p"/> Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, (into this mischief), and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth - When he meets with any thing that injures him; for God will not have thee to avenge thyself, or feel any disposition contrary to love; for if thou do, the Lord will be angry, and may turn away his wrath from him, and pour it out on thee. <div eID="gen24729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24730" type="x-p"/> This I believe to be the true sense of these verses: but we must return to the sixteenth, as that has been most sinfully misrepresented. <div eID="gen24730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24731" type="x-p"/> For a just man falleth seven times - That is, say many, "the most righteous man in the world sins seven times a day on an average." Solomon does not say so: - <div eID="gen24731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24732" type="x-p"/> 1. There is not a word about sin in the text. <div eID="gen24732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24733" type="x-p"/> 2. The word day is not in the Hebrew text, nor in any of the versions. <div eID="gen24733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24734" type="x-p"/> 3. The word יפול yippol, from נפל naphal, to fall, is never applied to sin. <div eID="gen24734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24735" type="x-p"/> 4. When set in opposition to the words riseth up, it merely applies to affliction or calamity. See <reference osisRef="Mic.7.8">Mic 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amo.8.4">Amo 8:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.27">Jer 25:27</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Psa.34.19">Psa 34:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.34.20">Psa 34:20</reference>. "The righteous falls into trouble." See above. <div eID="gen24735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24736" type="x-p"/> Mr. Holden has a very judicious note on this passage: "Injure not a righteous man; for, though he frequently falls into distress, yet, by the superintending care of Providence, 'he riseth up again,' is delivered from his distress, while the wicked are overwhelmed with their misfortunes. That this is the meaning is plain from the preceding and following verses: yet some expound it by the just man often relapsing into sin, and recovering from it; nay, it has even been adduced to prove the doctrine of the final perseverance of the elect. But נפל is never used for falling into sin, but into distress and affliction - as <reference osisRef="Pro.11.5">Pro 11:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Pro.11.14">Pro 11:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Pro.13.17">Pro 13:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Pro.17.20">Pro 17:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Pro.26.27">Pro 26:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Pro.28.10">Pro 28:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Pro.28.14">Pro 28:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Pro.28.18">Pro 28:18</reference>."
entries.42b9bac545f0fac151dafe60ba356aad40d4e39a: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen24736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24737" type="x-p"/> And he turn away his wrath from him - Wrath is here taken for the effect of wrath, punishment; and the meaning must be as paraphrased above - lest he take the punishment from him, and inflict it upon thee. And in this way Coverdale understood it: "Lest the Lorde be angry, and turn his wrath from him unto thee." Or we may understand it thus: Lest the Lord inflict on thee a similar punishment; for if thou get into his spirit, rejoicing in the calamities of another, thou deservest punishment.
entries.456d9e246c402235b23621c27a03c4665536256c: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen24737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24738" type="x-p"/> For there shall be no reboard to the evil man - אחרית acharith. There shall not be the future state of blessedness to the wicked. See the note on <reference osisRef="Pro.24.14">Pro 24:14</reference> (note). His candle shall be put out; his prosperity shall finally cease, or he shall have no posterity. Some have thought that this text intimates the annihilation of sinners; but it refers not to being, but to the state or condition of that being. The wicked shall be; but they shall not be Happy.
entries.518a667a3b7dfe43dad341bd4a17ca8361969a60: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen24738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24739" type="x-p"/> My son, fear thou the Lord and the king - Pay to each the homage due: to the Lord, Divine honor and adoration; to the king, civil respect, civil honor, and political obedience. <div eID="gen24739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24740" type="x-p"/> Meddle not with them that are given to change - עם שונים אל תתערב im shonim al titharab: "And with the changelings mingle not thyself." The innovators; those who are always for making experiments on modes of government, forms of religion, etc. The most dangerous spirit that can infect the human mind.
entries.e9ab80581610c0c06a973ca616c630c10cf31833: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen24740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24741" type="x-p"/> The ruin of them both? - Of them who do not fear the Lord; and of them that do not reverence the King.
entries.d3e9050ead1206a082cdeae0f256346ed349479c: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen24741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24742" type="x-p"/> These things also belong to the wise - גם אלה לחכמים gam elleh lachachamim, "These also to wise." This appears to be a new section; and perhaps, what follows belongs to another collection. Probably fragments of sayings collected by wise men from the Proverbs of Solomon. <div eID="gen24742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24743" type="x-p"/> It is not good to have respect - Judgment and justice should never be perverted.
entries.dac55f0960d1842583e5e33d17fcc8e570dc4c59: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen24743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24744" type="x-p"/> Kiss his lips - Shall treat him with affection and respect.
entries.6a42a0e3c7050131ec715dd034a1df72b1884cd1: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen24744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24745" type="x-p"/> Prepare thy work without - Do nothing without a plan. In winter prepare seed, implements, tackle, geers, etc., for seed-time and harvest.
entries.d3175fd4b8a14d409babfa1436b32cd7817e5584: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen24745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24746" type="x-p"/> Be not a witness - Do not be forward to offer thyself to bear testimony against a neighbor, in a matter which may prejudice him, where the essential claims of justice do not require such interference; and especially do not do this in a spirit of revenge, because he has injured thee before.
entries.2927c2879072e05aebea41c7abd0590ae51252a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen24746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24747" type="x-p"/> I went by the field of the slothful - This is a most instructive parable; is exemplified every day in a variety of forms; and is powerfully descriptive of the state of many a blackslider and trifler in religion. Calmet has an excellent note on this passage. I shall give the substance of it. <div eID="gen24747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24748" type="x-p"/> Solomon often recommends diligence and economy to his disciples. In those primitive times when agriculture was honorable, no man was respected who neglected to cultivate his grounds, who sunk into poverty, contracted debt, or engaged in ruinous securities. With great propriety, a principal part of wisdom was considered by them as consisting in the knowledge of properly conducting one's domestic affairs, and duly cultivating the inheritances derived from their ancestors. Moses had made a law to prevent the rich from utterly depressing the poor, by obliging them to return their farms to them on the Sabbatic year, and to remit all debts at the year of jubilee. <div eID="gen24748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24749" type="x-p"/> In the civil state of the Hebrews, we never see those enormous and suddenly raised fortunes, which never subsist but in the ruin of numberless families. One of the principal solicitudes of this legislator was to produce, as far as possible in a monarchical state, an equality of property and condition. The ancient Romans held agriculture in the same estimation, and highly respected those who had applied themselves to it with success. When they spoke in praise of a man, they considered themselves as giving no mean commendation when they called him a good husbandman, an excellent laborer. From such men they formed their most valiant generals and intrepid soldiers. Cato De Re Rustica, cap. 1. The property which is acquired by these means is most innocent, most solid, and exposes its possessor less to envy than property acquired in any other way. See Cicero De Officiis, lib. 1. In Britain the merchant is all in all; and yet the waves of the sea are not more uncertain, nor more tumultuous, than the property acquired in this way, or than the agitated life of the speculative merchant. <div eID="gen24749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24750" type="x-p"/> But let us look more particularly into this very instructive parable: - <div eID="gen24750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24751" type="x-p"/> I. The owner is described. <div eID="gen24751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24752" type="x-p"/> 1. He was איש עצל ish atsel, the loitering, sluggish, slothful man. <div eID="gen24752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24753" type="x-p"/> 2. He was אדם חסר לב adam chasar leb, a man that wanted heart; destitute of courage, alacrity, and decision of mind. <div eID="gen24753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24754" type="x-p"/> II. His circumstances. This man had, <div eID="gen24754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24755" type="x-p"/> 1. שדה sadeh, a sowed field, arable ground. This was the character of his estate. It was meadow and corn land. <div eID="gen24755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24756" type="x-p"/> 2. He had כרם kerem, a vineyard, what we would call perhaps garden and orchard, where he might employ his skill to great advantage in raising various kinds of fruits and culinary herbs for the support of his family. <div eID="gen24756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24757" type="x-p"/> III. The state of this heritage: <div eID="gen24757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24758" type="x-p"/> 1. "It was grown over with thorns." It had been long neglected, so that even brambles were permitted to grow in the fields: <div eID="gen24758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24759" type="x-p"/> 2. "Nettles had covered the face thereof." It was not weeded, and all kinds of rubbish had been suffered to multiply: <div eID="gen24759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24760" type="x-p"/> 3. "The stone wall was broken down." This belonged to the vineyard: it was neither pruned nor digged; and the fence, for want of timely repairs, had all fallen into ruins, <reference osisRef="Pro.24.31">Pro 24:31</reference>. <div eID="gen24760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24761" type="x-p"/> IV. The effect all this had on the attentive observer. <div eID="gen24761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24762" type="x-p"/> 1. I saw it, אחזה אנכי echezeh anochi, I fixed my attention on it. I found it was no mere report. It is a fact. I myself was an eyewitness of it. <div eID="gen24762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24763" type="x-p"/> 2. I considered it well, אשית לבי ashith libbi, I put my heart on it. All my feelings were interested. <div eID="gen24763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24764" type="x-p"/> 3. I looked upon it, רעיתי raithi, I took an intellectual view of it. And <div eID="gen24764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24765" type="x-p"/> 4. Thus I received instruction, לקחתי מוסר lakachti musar, I received a very important lesson from it: but the owner paid no attention to it. He alone was uninstructed; for he "slumbered, slept, and kept his hands in his bosom." <reference osisRef="Pro.24.33">Pro 24:33</reference>. "Hugged himself in his sloth and carelessness." <div eID="gen24765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24766" type="x-p"/> V. The consequences of this conduct. <div eID="gen24766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24767" type="x-p"/> 1. Poverty described as coming like a traveler, making sure steps every hour coming nearer and nearer to the door. <div eID="gen24767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24768" type="x-p"/> 2. Want, מחסר machsor, total destitution; want of all the necessaries, conveniences, and comforts of life; and this is described as coming like an armed man כאיש מגן keish magen, as a man with a shield, who comes to destroy this unprofitable servant: or it may refer to a man coming with what we call an execution into the house, armed with the law, to take even his bed from the slumberer. <div eID="gen24768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24769" type="x-p"/> From this literal solution any minister of God may make a profitable discourse.  <chapter eID="Prov.24"/> <div eID="gen24769" type="x-p"/>

entries.3da324287eb69ac8e0c0d1424c3326b07e3508a2: <reference osisRef="Prov.24.1-Prov.24.2">Pro 24:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen11562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11563" type="x-p"/> After this divergence (in <reference osisRef="Prov.23.29-Prov.23.35">Pro 23:29-35</reference>) from the usual form of the proverb, there is now a return to the tetrastich: 1 Envy not evil men,    And desire not to have intercourse with them. 2 For their heart thinketh of violence,    And their lips speak mischief. <div eID="gen11563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11564" type="x-p"/> The warning, not to envy the godless, is also found at <reference osisRef="Prov.3.31">Pro 3:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.23.17">Pro 23:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.19">Pro 24:19</reference>, but is differently constructed in each of these passages. Regarding תּתאו with <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 23:3. אנשׁי רעה (cf. רע, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.5">Pro 28:5</reference>) are the wicked, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, such as cleave to evil, and to whom evil clings. The warning is grounded in this, that whoever have intercourse with such men, make themselves partners in greater sins and evil: for their heart broodeth (write כּי שׁד, <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>) violence, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, robbery, plunder, destruction, murder, and the like. With שׁד (in the <hi type="italic">Mishle</hi> only here and at <reference osisRef="Prov.21.7">Pro 21:7</reference>, cf. שׁדּד, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.26">Pro 19:26</reference>) connects itself elsewhere חמס, here (cf. <reference osisRef="Hab.1.3">Hab 1:3</reference>) עמל, <hi type="italic">labor, molestia</hi>, viz., those who prepare it for others by means of slanderous, crafty, uncharitable talk.
entries.62f7b1738cc576593c61e8fa995be0399672b76a: <reference osisRef="Prov.24.3-Prov.24.4">Pro 24:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen11564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11565" type="x-p"/> The warning against fellowship with the godless is followed by the praise of wisdom, which is rooted in the fear of God. 3 By wisdom is the house builded,    And by understanding is it established. 4 And by knowledge shall the chambers be filled    With all manner of precious and pleasant goods. <div eID="gen11565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11566" type="x-p"/> What is meant by the “building of the house” is explained at Pro 14:1. It is wisdom, viz., that which originates from God, which is rooted in fellowship with Him, by which every household, be it great or small, prospers and attains to a successful and flourishing state; כּונן, as parallel word to בּנה (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.19">Pro 3:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.2.12">Pro 2:12</reference>), is related to it as <hi type="italic">statuere</hi> to <hi type="italic">extruere</hi>; the <hi type="italic">Hithpal</hi> (as at Num 21:17) means to keep oneself in a state of continuance, to gain perpetuity, to become established. That ימּלאוּ by <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi> has not passed over into the pausal ימּלאוּ, arises from this, that the <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>, by the poetical system of accents, has only the force of the prose accent <hi type="italic">Sakef</hi>; the clause completes itself only by 4b; the pausal form on that account also is not found, and it is discontinued, because the <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi> does not produce any pausal effect (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Ps.45.6">Psa 45:6</reference>). The form of expression in <reference osisRef="Prov.24.4">Pro 24:4</reference> is like <reference osisRef="Prov.1.13">Pro 1:13</reference>; Pro 3:10. But the חדרים, of storerooms (lxx as <reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Isa 26:20</reference>, ταμιεῖα), and נעים, like <reference osisRef="Prov.22.18">Pro 22:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.23.8">Pro 23:8</reference>, is peculiar to this collection.
entries.83285734bce30eadf0a805b4789c4df9b64e8539: <reference osisRef="Prov.24.5-Prov.24.6">Pro 24:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen11566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11567" type="x-p"/> The praise of wisdom is continued: it brings blessings in the time of peace, and gives the victory in war. 5 A wise man is full of strength;    And a man of understanding showeth great power. 6 For with wise counsel shalt thou carry on successful war;    And safety is where counsellors are not wanting. <div eID="gen11567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11568" type="x-p"/> The ב of בּעוז (thus with <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi> in old impressions, Cod. 1294, Cod. <hi type="italic">Jaman</hi>., and elsewhere with the Masoretic note לית ומלא) introduces, as that of בכּח, <reference osisRef="Ps.24.4">Psa 24:4</reference>, the property in which a person or thing appears; the article (cf. העזבים, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.13">Pro 2:13</reference>, Gesen, §35, 2A) is that of gender. The parallel מאמץ כח, a Greek translates by ὑπὲρ κραταιὸν ἰσχύΐ = מאמּיץ כּח (<reference osisRef="Job.9.4">Job 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.26">Isa 40:26</reference>). But after 5a it lies nearer that the poet means to express the power which lies in wisdom itself (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.19">Ecc 7:19</reference>), and its superiority to physical force (<reference osisRef="Prov.21.22">Pro 21:22</reference>); the lxx, Syr., and Targ. also, it is true, translate 5a as if מעז (<hi type="italic">prae potente</hi>) were the words used. אמּץ כּח means to strengthen the strength, and that is (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.2">Nah 2:2</reference>) equivalent to, to collect the strength (to take courage), here and at <reference osisRef="Amos.2.14">Amo 2:14</reference>, to show strong (superior) strength. The reason is gathered from <reference osisRef="Prov.20.18">Pro 20:18</reference> and Pro 11:14. The לך here added, Hitzig is determined to read תּעשׂה: for with prudent counsel the war shall be carried out by thee. The construction of the passive with ל of the subject is correct in Heb. (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.14.20">Pro 14:20</reference>) as well as in Aram.,<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Nöldeke’s <hi type="italic">Neusyrische Gram</hi>. p. 219, <hi type="italic">Anm</hi>., and p. 416.</note> and עשׂה frequently means, in a pregnant sense: to complete, to carry out, to bring to an end; but the phrase עשׂה מלחמה means always to carry on war, and nothing further. לך is the <hi type="italic">dat. commod</hi>., as in נלחם ל, to wage war (to contend) for any one, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Exo 14:14. Instead of ברב, the lxx reads בלב; regarding γεωργίου μεγάλου for מאמץ כח, without doubt a corrupt reading, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Lagarde.
entries.e952c42d691a8d38f6c852a0b551fbedd34e3343: <reference osisRef="Prov.24.7">Pro 24:7</reference> <div eID="gen11568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11569" type="x-p"/> Till now in this appendix we have found only two distichs (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., vol. i. p. 17); now several of them follow. From this, that wisdom is a power which accomplishes great things, it follows that it is of high value, though to the fool it appears all too costly. 7 Wisdom seems to the fool to be an ornamental commodity;    He openeth not his mouth in the gate. <div eID="gen11569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11570" type="x-p"/> Most interpreters take ראמות for רמות (written as at <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.58">1Ch 6:58</reference>; cf. Zec 14:10; ראשׁ, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.4">Pro 10:4</reference>; קאם, Hos 10:14), and translate, as Jerome and Luther: “Wisdom is to the fool too high;” the way to wisdom is to him too long and too steep, the price too costly, and not to be afforded. Certainly this thought does not lie far distant from what the poet would say; but why does he say חכמות, and not חכמה? This חכמות is not a numerical plur., so as to be translated with the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>.: μετέωροι τῷ ἄφρονι αἱ ἐπιστῆμαι; it is a plur., as <reference osisRef="Ps.49.4">Psa 49:4</reference> shows; but, as is evident from the personification and the construction, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.20">Pro 1:20</reference>, one inwardly multiplying and heightening, which is related to חכמה as science or the contents of knowledge is to knowledge. That this plur. comes here into view as in chap. 1-9 (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., vol. i. p. 34), is definitely accounted for in these chapters by the circumstance that wisdom was to be designated, which is the <hi type="italic">mediatrix</hi> of all wisdom; here, to be designated in intentional symphony with ראמות, whose plur. ending <hi type="italic">ôth</hi> shall be for that very reason, however, inalienable. Thus ראמות will be the name of a costly foreign <hi type="italic">bijouterie</hi>, which is mentioned in the Book of Job, where the unfathomableness and inestimableness of wisdom is celebrated; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Job.27.18">Job 27:18</reference>, where we have recorded what we had to say at the time regarding this word. But what is now the meaning of the saying that wisdom is to the fool a pearl or precious coral? Joël Bril explains: “The fool uses the sciences like a precious stone, only for ornament, but he knows not how to utter a word publicly,” This is to be rejected, because ראמות is not so usual a trinket or ornament as to serve as an expression of this thought. The third of the comparison lies in the rarity, costliness, unattainableness; the fool despises wisdom, because the expenditure of strength and the sacrifices of all kinds which are necessary to put one into the possession of wisdom deter him from it (Rashi). This is also the sense which the expression has when ראמות = רמות; and probably for the sake of this double meaning the poet chose just this word, and not פנינים, גבישׁ, or any other name, for articles of ornament (Hitzig). The Syr. has incorrectly interpreted this play upon words: <hi type="italic">sapientia abjecta stulto</hi>; and the Targumist: the fool grumbles (מתרעם) against wisdom.<note placement="foot">This explanation is more correct than Levy's: he lifts himself up (boasts) with wisdom.</note> <div eID="gen11570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11571" type="x-p"/> He may also find the grapes to be sour because they hang too high for him; here it is only said that wisdom remains at a distance from him because he cannot soar up to its attainment; for that very reason he does not open his mouth in the gate, where the council and the representatives of the people have their seats: he has not the knowledge necessary for being associated in counselling, and thus must keep silent; and this is indeed the most prudent thing he can do.
entries.584683b16b3a4f8516b03841cb88375761a08c61: <reference osisRef="Prov.24.8">Pro 24:8</reference> <div eID="gen11571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11572" type="x-p"/> From wisdom, which is a moral good, the following proverb passes over to a kind of σοφία δαιμονιώδης: <div eID="gen11572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11573" type="x-p"/> He that meditateth to do evil, <div eID="gen11573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11574" type="x-p"/> We call such an one an intriguer. <div eID="gen11574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11575" type="x-p"/> A verbal explanation and definition like <reference osisRef="Prov.21.24">Pro 21:24</reference> (cf. p. 29), formed like <reference osisRef="Prov.16.21">Pro 16:21</reference> from נבון. Instead of בּעל־מזמּות [lord of mischief] in <reference osisRef="Prov.12.2">Pro 12:2</reference>, the expression is 'אישׁ מ (cf. at <reference osisRef="Prov.22.24">Pro 22:24</reference>). Regarding מזמות in its usual sense, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Pro 5:2. Such definitions have of course no lexicographical, but only a moral aim. That which is here given is designed to warn one against gaining for himself this ambiguous title of a refined (cunning, <hi type="italic">versutus</hi>) man; one is so named whose schemes and endeavours are directed to the doing of evil. One may also inversely find the turning-point of the warning in 8b: “he who projects deceitful plans against the welfare of others, finds his punishment in this, that he falls under public condemnation as a worthless intriguer” (Elster). But מזמות is a ῥῆμα μέσον, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.5.2">Pro 5:2</reference>; the title is thus equivocal, and the turning-point lies in the bringing out of his kernel: מחשּׁב להרע = meditating to do evil.
